nameStory: The spotted-winged grasshopper gets its name from the distinctive dark spots or bands that decorate its wings, which become visible when it takes flight or spreads its wings while sunbathing. These wing markings help distinguish it from many other grasshoppers that have plain or differently patterned wings. The scientific name Orphulella comes from a diminutive form meaning 'little orphan,' perhaps referring to its relatively small size among grasshoppers.
description: The spotted-winged grasshopper is a small to medium-sized grasshopper belonging to the slant-faced group, recognizable by its angled face profile. This nimble hopper typically measures about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a streamlined body built for quick escapes. Its most distinctive feature is the spotted or banded pattern on its wings, which flash into view when it jumps or flies. Like all grasshoppers, it has powerful hind legs for jumping and chews plant material with strong mandibles.

idTips.label: Spotted Wings
idTips.description: Look for dark spots or bands across the wings, especially visible when the grasshopper spreads them or takes short flights - the wings feel papery and delicate to the touch if you can catch one

idTips.label: Slanted Face
idTips.description: The face angles backward from top to bottom rather than being vertical, giving it a distinctive wedge-shaped profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Relatively small and slender compared to chunky field crickets, with a smooth, streamlined body that feels firm but not heavily armored

idTips.label: Jumping Behavior
idTips.description: Makes quick, darting jumps when disturbed, often landing a few feet away with a soft patting sound on leaves or grass

idTips.label: Body Coloration
idTips.description: Usually brownish or grayish with mottled patterns that help it blend with dried grass and soil, feeling smooth and slightly waxy to the touch

habitat: Spotted-winged grasshoppers prefer open, grassy areas including meadows, prairies, old fields, and grassland edges throughout New England. They're often found in areas with mixed grasses and low-growing plants, particularly where the soil is well-drained and gets plenty of sunlight. You'll commonly spot them in unmowed areas along roadsides, in pastures, and in the grassy margins of agricultural fields.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs laid the previous fall are developing in the soil and won't hatch until warmer weather arrives.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - adults are jumping, mating, and most easily observed on warm, sunny days when they're actively feeding and moving through grass.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with females laying eggs in soil before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: No adults present; the species overwinters as eggs buried in soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger hatching.

funFact: Spotted-winged grasshoppers can actually 'sing' by rubbing their hind legs against their wings, but their songs are so high-pitched that many adult humans can't hear them - it's like having a secret grasshopper radio frequency playing in the meadows around us!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small grasshoppers in grassy areas, but the spotted wing pattern is your best clue - many similar grasshoppers have plain wings or different patterns. Remember: 'Spotted wings, spotted right!' when trying to identify this species among the many brown grasshoppers hopping around.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'short-horned grasshopper' refers to their relatively short antennae compared to crickets and katydids, which are 'long-horned' - this has nothing to do with actual horns but is an old naming convention that can confuse beginners learning to tell these jumping insects apart.
compareHints: The spotted-winged grasshopper differs from its close relative, the pasture locust (Orphulella speciosa), primarily in its wing markings - the pasture locust typically has clearer, less spotted wings. Both share the characteristic slanted face profile of their genus, but the spotted-winged grasshopper's wing patterns are more pronounced and consistent, making it easier to identify when you get a good look at the wings in flight or when the insect is at rest with wings slightly spread.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Pasture Locust differs from its close relative, the Spotted-winged Grasshopper, by having plainer wing markings and preferring drier habitats.
